newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Chinas policy on HK undermines confidence-Rifkind.
newsitem.headline: Chinas policy on HK undermines confidence-Rifkind.

text.p: The only way China can restore confidence in Hong Kong is to reverse its policy of unwinding democratic reforms and dismantling the elected legislature, British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Saturday.
Rifkind, who flew into Hong Kong for a visit cut short by the need to return to London for a key parliamentary vote, said he had put these views to his Chinese counterpart.
"I was pleased yesterday when I saw (Chinese Vice Premier and Foreign Minister) Qian Qichen to be able to speak directly to him on these anxieties and concerns," Rifkind told reporters.

"We have been able to make clear that these are aspects of Chinese policy which inevitably have damaged confidence in the territory and the only way that that confidence can be fully restored is by a fundamental change in that policy."
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
Rifkind lands in the midst of a bitter political quarrel over the future of democratic elections and human rights laws, which China plans to scratch after July 1.

Beijing argues its plan to install a provisional legislature in place of the elected legislative chamber and roll back key elements of Hong Kongs civil liberties, including part of its bill of rights, would not materially affect freedoms.
Rifkind said Britain had "challenged the Chinese authorities that if they believe in the justification for the provisional legislature to join with us in taking it to the international court.
"But the Chinese did not wish to respond to that proposal."

A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman said Qian declared the issue closed during the one-and-a-half hour meeting with Rifkind in Singapore where both men were attending a meeting of European and Asian foreign ministers.
Rifkind said afterwards it would be "naive and unrealistic" to expect China to make concessions on the issue but warned of a groundswell of international concern about Chinas plans.
Rifkind has an appointment to meet Hong Kongs future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, on Sunday and will hold talks with politicians and Governor Chris Pattens key advisers.

Political tempers flared this week when Tung launched blistering attacks on the territorys Democratic Party, which he said had blackened Hong Kongs name overseas by spreading doomsday predictions about the loss of freedoms.
Tung, chosen by a China-backed Selection Committee last month, argues the planned changes are merely technicalities.

Rifkind flies back to London early on Monday for a vote called by the opposition Labour Party over the governments handling of the "mad cow" disease crisis, which if lost could trigger an opposition motion of no confidence in John Majors government.
